prereqs: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
lesson:
# The device-model seam

The device-model interface is the simulator's most important seam. The core asks one question per device per iteration: given these terminal voltages, temperature and parameters, what are the currents, charges and their derivatives? Everything model-specific lives behind that question. Designing the seam well, and testing what passes through it, is what lets new transistor models arrive as plug-ins instead of core edits.

## What the device interface returns

For each device the core supplies terminal voltages, temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode. The model returns terminal currents, which form the Newton residual; their derivatives with respect to terminal voltages, which form the Jacobian; terminal charges, which the integrator differentiates so that charge is conserved; charge derivatives, the capacitances used in transient and AC; and, in noise analysis, its noise source densities. A MOSFET returning $g_m$, $g_{ds}$ and $I_{eq}$ at an iterate is exactly this contract. A narrow, stable interface like this lets the core treat a diode and a BSIM transistor identically, as stamps.

## Adding a model as a plug-in

A new model, typically written in Verilog-A, is compiled into code that implements the device interface and loads at run time, leaving the solver untouched: a Tier 2 change. Good plug-ins follow the seam rules: no hidden global state, so results are deterministic and order-independent; a frozen extension ABI, so compiled models survive simulator releases; and coarse calls, evaluating many instances of one model per call. A plug-in whose currents are right but whose derivatives have a sign error still converges to the right answer, because the residual uses the currents, but Newton slows or fails, which is why derivative correctness is a separate test.

## Testing a new device model

Device-level tests check the interface contract: compare the returned Jacobian with finite differences of the returned currents at many bias points; check continuity and source-drain symmetry near $V_{DS} = 0$, where many models kink and cause convergence failures and wrong distortion; and, for a speed-optimized rewrite, compare currents, charges and derivatives with the reference model over a grid of biases and temperatures. Circuit-level golden tests then catch what device tests miss, such as charge errors: if a ring oscillator built from the model runs 5% faster than its golden result, promotion is blocked, and the golden value is not updated to match.

## Going deeper

McAndrew et al., "Best practices for compact modeling in Verilog-A" (IEEE Journal of the Electron Devices Society, 2015); the Xyce Users' Guide, on device models.

problems.q:
Which context should a device-model seam expose to the model, beyond terminal voltages?

A) The plotting settings

B) The other devices' internal state

C) Temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode, such as DC, transient, AC or noise

D) The full netlist text
problems.a: Temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode, such as DC, transient, AC or noise
problems.e: Models depend on temperature and geometry and must provide extra data in some analyses, such as noise sources in noise analysis.

problems.q:
Why should the device interface also return noise sources?

A) Noise analysis needs each device's noise power densities to propagate them to the output

B) To randomize the transient

C) To report Monte Carlo statistics

D) To set gmin
problems.a: Noise analysis needs each device's noise power densities to propagate them to the output
problems.e: Noise analysis sums device noise through transfer functions, so each model reports its thermal, shot and flicker densities at the operating point.

problems.q:
Why does the device interface return charges rather than capacitances for transient?

A) Charges make the matrix symmetric

B) The integrator differentiates charge, which conserves it for nonlinear capacitances

C) Transient analysis has no Jacobian

D) Capacitances cannot be represented as numbers
problems.a: The integrator differentiates charge, which conserves it for nonlinear capacitances
problems.e: A charge-based interface lets the core apply any integration rule to $q(v)$ and keeps charge conserved.

problems.q:
A team writes a new transistor model in Verilog-A. How does it typically reach a SPICE-class simulator without editing the simulator core?

A) It replaces the LU solver

B) It is pasted into the Newton loop

C) A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface

D) It is converted to a .options card
problems.a: A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface
problems.e: Compiled Verilog-A plug-ins, for example through standardized compiled-model interfaces, implement the device seam while the core stays fixed.

problems.q:
A plug-in model computes currents correctly but its derivatives contain a sign error. What will the simulator show?

A) A syntax error at load time

B) Slow or failed Newton convergence, while any converged answer is still correct

C) Faster convergence

D) Wrong converged voltages
problems.a: Slow or failed Newton convergence, while any converged answer is still correct
problems.e: The residual uses the currents, so a converged solution satisfies KCL. A wrong Jacobian only degrades the Newton iterations.

problems.q:
A team writes a new transistor model in Verilog-A. How does it typically reach a SPICE-class simulator without editing the simulator core?

A) It is converted to a .options card

B) A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface

C) It replaces the LU solver

D) It is pasted into the Newton loop
problems.a: A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface
problems.e: Compiled Verilog-A plug-ins, for example through standardized compiled-model interfaces, implement the device seam while the core stays fixed.

problems.q:
Which automated check catches a derivative bug in a new device plug-in?

A) Comparing node names

B) Running one DC point

C) Checking that the model compiles

D) Comparing the returned Jacobian with finite differences of the returned currents at many bias points
problems.a: Comparing the returned Jacobian with finite differences of the returned currents at many bias points
problems.e: A finite-difference Jacobian check exercises exactly the interface contract and flags inconsistent derivatives before they slow Newton.

problems.q:
A plug-in model shows a discontinuity in drain current at Vds = 0 when tested. Why test that point specifically?

A) It is the only point with nonzero current

B) It tests the timestep control

C) Vds = 0 is never simulated

D) Symmetry and continuity at Vds = 0 are where many models fail, causing Newton and distortion problems
problems.a: Symmetry and continuity at Vds = 0 are where many models fail, causing Newton and distortion problems
problems.e: Source-drain symmetry tests near Vds = 0 are standard model quality checks, because kinks there cause convergence failures and wrong harmonic distortion.

problems.q:
A model passes its device-level tests, but a ring oscillator built from it runs 5% faster than the golden result. What should happen?

A) Update the golden result to match

B) Block promotion and investigate, since circuit-level golden tests disagree

C) Promote it, since device tests passed

D) Loosen the tolerance to 6%
problems.a: Block promotion and investigate, since circuit-level golden tests disagree
problems.e: Golden circuit tests catch interactions device tests miss, such as charge errors. A failed golden check blocks promotion.
